0: The strongest image- and video-generation models right now are probably GPT Images 2.5 and Seedance 2.5, which have pushed the ceiling for both a notch higher.
1: So if those are the front runners among closed models, what level are open models at now? Are they toys? Can they really deliver productivity?
2: This piece looks at just how far the experts have taken open models. For images we pick Alibaba's Z-Image, and for video, MiniMax H3.
4: Z-Image is a 6B image-generation model under the Apache 2.0 licence. The complete Z-Image is a non-distilled base model supporting CFG, negative prompts and fine-tuning; in the community the more common one is Z-Image-Turbo, which uses only 8 steps and is all about speed.
5: MiniMax H3 is a 33B audio-video generation model that can output 4 to 15 seconds at 24 fps with stereo audio. Strictly speaking it is an open-weights model under the MiniMax H3 Community Licence. The released H3-Base can generate 768p audio-video locally, but the official Context-IR that handles complex input, and the 2K regeneration pipeline, are not fully open-sourced.
7: Many image models today can generate a pretty woman, and a single retouched face on its own is not very interesting. What is genuinely hard is: is the text spelled right? Is the count right? Does the same product stay consistent across different views? Are complex spatial relations understood correctly?
8: First, a set of local tests by @witcheer.
9: He ran Z-Image-Turbo on an RTX 5090; a 1024px image takes about 3.2 seconds. The prompt required the shop sign to spell out a given word and to draw “exactly three ducks”, and both the text and the count came out right.
10: Those two tasks look childish, but they have long been the hard problems of diffusion models. Letters blur easily, and three ducks often end up as four or five.
12: Next, a case closer to e-commerce delivery.
13: @rizavelioglu had the model generate a split image: a white patterned T-shirt alone on the left, and on the right a real model wearing the same garment. The prompt also required the print, text, fabric, stitching and cut to be preserved.
14: In the final image the two sides were not drawn as separate garments: the pattern and cut largely match. For an e-commerce team that is worth far more than generating a single “pretty model photo”. Product shots, on-body shots and marketing images can all continue from the same design.
15: Of course this is one successful sample, still some way from reliable batch output. But it at least shows the direction works.
17: On photorealistic portraits, @dreamydigiarts ran a comparison with the same prompt.
18: He had Z-Image-Turbo and Nano Banana 2 both generate a low-angle phone shot: blue sky, backlighting, a person leaning back holding a large bunch of wild flowers, hair blown by the wind, and the slight grain of a phone photo preserved.
19: Z-Image's image already has a strong snapshot feel. The jeans, skin and backlighting do not blur into a layer of plastic, and the low-angle composition holds up. For mood portraits or social-media images it is no longer toy-grade at all.
21: Z-Image is not only photorealistic either. @tisch_eins tested Boogu, Flux 2 Klein and Z-Image-Turbo with the same prompt. The scene called for a black-haired sorceress standing on a stormy mountain peak, a golden staff that must appear complete from hand to tip, a bolt of lightning shooting from the staff tip into the clouds, plus a low camera angle, a full-body composition, cloak, runes, arcs of electricity and strong golden rim light.
22: A prompt like that easily fails on one thing or another: the staff gets cropped, the lightning attaches in the wrong place, or the figure shrinks to a big head. Z-Image's result keeps the main relationships intact, which shows strong control over complex illustrative compositions too.
24: Last is an extreme macro. @aisthetiic's prompt is very short: let some animal's pupil fill the frame, light it with dramatic light from the upper left to reveal the iris texture, and make the background a blurred gradient from dark to bright.
25: What is more interesting is that the image does not fall apart. The eye is locked firmly on the pupil, and the light, shadow and background all serve the same subject. For a poster key visual or a moody cover, that kind of compositional discipline is more useful than piling on a thousand phrases like “8K, masterpiece, ultra-detailed”.
27: Seen together, these five cases make Z-Image's strengths fairly clear:
28: The model is small, fast, solid at photorealism, and able to follow fairly long natural language. The complete base model can go on to LoRA, ControlNet and industry fine-tuning.
30: Video generation is far harder than image generation: a wrong finger in an image can sometimes be cropped out, but in video, if a character's face changes within 15 seconds, the camera does not follow the timeline, a line goes to the wrong person, or the sound does not match the action, the whole clip is ruined.
31: Among the H3 cases, the first worth seeing is two-character consistency.
32: @coolthor fed two character design images generated by Z-Image into H3's Ref2VA mode. One wears an ochre robe, the other blue-grey clothes, deliberately different in look. The prompt has one character enter at second 6 to 8, and includes three lines of Chinese dialogue.
33: In the 10.125-second video the two do not swap faces or clothes. The character due to enter does not appear in the first half, arriving at about second 7. The author also checked the 44 Chinese characters with ASR: a 6.8% character error rate, and the errors were homophones.
34: This one ran on a single RTX 5090: 243 frames took 437 seconds. Not very fast, but controlling characters, timing and dialogue together is already impressive.

38: Using an RTX 4090 and ComfyUI he tried three things: a four-scene travel short, a music video cutting on the drum beat, and a seaside story with four shots and ambient sound. The raw idea goes first to MiniMax's official Prompt Writing Skill, which turns it into a structured prompt with shots, timing, action and sound, and that goes to H3.
39: The most useful thing here is that it does not just make the image “quite pretty”. When the beat lands, the image really cuts; in the seaside one, four shots, mood and background sound come out together in one pass.
40: His measured figures: on a 4090, a 15-second, 20-step low-resolution video takes over 200 seconds; at 768p it takes over 1000 seconds. Open source lets you iterate, but free does not mean costless — electricity, VRAM and waiting time are costs too.

43: @PixelAigc's 30-second Jane Eyre-style English manor piece is even more striking.
44: His prompt splits the 30 seconds into four shots. Each one specifies focal length, camera position, blocking, micro-expressions, dialogue, breathing, ambient sound and forbidden items. The character's emotion moves from testing to pushing back to being moved, and the male and female voices are constrained separately.
45: This clip used local ComfyUI and an H3 Turbo LoRA, output at 480p first and then upscaled to 1080p with Topaz. The author's timing: about 13 to 15 minutes for 25 seconds. It does not represent a bare run of the official model, but it does represent the most interesting thing about the open ecosystem: a month after release, the community is already changing the speed, making long videos and wiring in automatic upscaling.

48: H3's official limit is 15 seconds per segment, so how do you make longer videos?
49: @superalesha ran a 30-second first-person action film on four RTX 3090s. He chained two 15-second segments: the first deliberately ends on a stable frame, the second is generated from the same frame, then the duplicate frames are cut and the audio continues.
50: The seam in the final film hides at second 15 and is hard to spot in normal viewing. The whole film took 44 minutes from generation to completion. The value of this case is not that H3 suddenly broke the duration limit, but that someone understood the limit and worked around it with a workflow.

53: There is also a case particularly good for studying “how should video prompts be written”.
54: @ou_zhen599 made a 15-second cyber spaceship short with local ComfyUI. The scene has three female characters: one seated on the left throughout, one standing in the middle holding a knife, one standing front-right holding a soda can. The prompt does not just give the plot: it states who speaks at which second, that those not speaking must not move their lips, that the can must stay in the right hand, when the red tracking dot appears on screen, and finally the shadow outside the porthole pressing in.
55: The hardest part of such a case is keeping the space tidy, not losing props, not crossing the dialogue and actually keeping silent characters silent. H3 can already execute that many constraints in one 15-second short, and the way open video is played has clearly changed.

59: If you just want the fastest single finished clip, closed models are still less hassle.
60: But if you want to iterate, generate in batches, train your own style, or put the capability into a local workflow, Z-Image and H3 are already worth studying seriously. Use the open models to try out shots and material, and call a closed model when you are truly stuck — the cost will be much lower.
61: Open models used to feel like a cheap stand-in you wait for; now they can take part in real creative work.
62: For people who make images and videos every day, the most satisfying change is that from now on, every time an idea appears, you do not first have to work out how many credits this round will burn.
